title: I built a crypto signal journal for trading communities — RED TEAM
author: MojtabaWEB
selftext:
I built RED TEAM, a browser-based prototype designed to help crypto traders track signals and evaluate their own trading performance.

The idea is simple: instead of relying only on a signal channel's reported results, traders can record their own entries, exits, position sizes and outcomes.

**Features currently included:**

* LONG/SHORT signal tracking
* Entry, stop-loss and take-profit levels
* Leverage and risk-based position sizing estimates
* Personal trade history and performance statistics
* Manual exit recording and CSV export
* A searchable archive of reported community signals

**Live demo:** [https://mojtaba-w.github.io/RED-TEAM/](https://mojtaba-w.github.io/RED-TEAM/)

The current version runs in the browser and stores personal entries locally. The archive records reported outcomes from exported messages; those outcomes have not been independently verified. It does not yet have shared team accounts, a backend database or a live market feed.

I'm looking for feedback from traders and developers:

Would a tool like this be more useful as a personal trading journal, a community dashboard, or both?

What would you improve first?

This is an independent prototype, and I'm exploring how to develop it into a more useful product.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: journal, and the column I'd add first is the price you actually got next to the price the signal called. on fast crypto calls that gap eats more than people expect, and a channel's own results never show it.

replies.author: MojtabaWEB
replies.body: That's a really good point. Comparing the signal price with the actual execution price would make the journal much more useful, especially for fast-moving crypto markets. A channel's reported P&L doesn't necessarily reflect what followers can actually achieve after slippage and fees. I'll add this to the feature priorities. Appreciate the suggestion!

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: fees are the easy half since they barely change, slippage is the one that moves. logging the seconds between the call and your fill would show how much of the gap is just being late.

replies.author: MojtabaWEB
replies.body: Great point. Tracking the time between signal receipt and actual execution would add useful context to slippage analysis. It could help distinguish execution delays from other factors like market volatility and liquidity. I’ll add signal-to-fill delay tracking to the roadmap alongside actual execution prices and fees. Thanks for the insight!

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: bucket the delay by time of day when you add it. the same channel can look fine at 2pm and awful in the first ten minutes after the open, and one average hides that.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Tracking your own fills against the channel’s reported results is the most useful thing a signal journal can do, and saying the archive outcomes aren’t verified is the right caveat. I’d build it as a personal journal first, with three fields on every entry: the time the signal was posted, the time you actually entered, and the fill price, so the delay and slippage are measured per trade. A comparison of the channel’s reported results against the average user’s fills, with the trade count, would show whether a channel’s edge survives after costs. Funding Rate Radar at Cymetica shows perp funding across venues, which is one cost that signal channels rarely include in reported results.

replies.author: MojtabaWEB
replies.body: Thanks for the thoughtful feedback! That’s exactly the direction I want to take RED TEAM — focusing on real-world execution rather than just reported signal performance. I’ve started adding signal timestamps, actual entry times, fill prices, execution delay, slippage, and fees to the personal journal. The next step is to compare reported results with actual user outcomes, while being transparent about sample sizes and unverified historical data. Funding rates are a great point too. They can have a meaningful impact on perp trade profitability, so incorporating them would make the performance analysis more realistic. Appreciate the suggestions — this is really helpful feedback!
